title: Can a Christian Be Rich?
excerpt: Jesus said harder things about wealth than most churches repeat, the church has never agreed on how far those words reach, and both the prosperity preacher and his proudest critic have something to answer for.
body:
Money is the subject Christians lie to each other about most politely. A couple sits in church with a house larger than they need and a quiet unease they have never mentioned to anyone, because they aren't sure whether what they feel is conviction or just nerves. A few rows back sits a man who works two jobs and has been told, by a preacher on his phone, that his rent would be paid if his faith were stronger and his offering larger. And somewhere nearby is a person who has never had much, who has come to believe that this makes him better than the people who have, and who would be offended to hear that Jesus might have a word for him too.

Each of them has a slogan. Money is a blessing. Money is the root of all evil. God wants you to prosper. Blessed are the poor. Every one of those is a piece of something the Bible says, pulled loose from the rest, and people fight over the pieces.

Most of us reading this are rich. We don't feel rich, because we compare ourselves with the people just above us. But by the standards of nearly everyone who has ever lived, and of much of the world today, a household with clean water, a full refrigerator, a car and some savings is wealthy. When Jesus talks about the rich, a good share of his American readers should stop looking around the room.

## What Jesus Said

Jesus talked about money constantly, and what he said is more severe than we usually let it be.

A man ran up to him once and knelt, asking how to inherit eternal life. He had kept the commandments since he was young. Mark records what happened next with a detail that is easy to pass over: "And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, 'You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me'" (Mark 10:21). The man went away grieving, "for he had great possessions" (10:22). Then Jesus turned to his disciples and said the line that people have been trying to shrink ever since: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God" (10:25).

The shrinking usually takes the form of a story about a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye, which a camel could squeeze through on its knees. No ancient source mentions any such gate. Jesus picked the largest animal his hearers knew and the smallest opening they knew, and he meant what it sounds like. The disciples understood him. They "were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, 'Then who can be saved?'" (10:26). In their world, as in ours, wealth looked like evidence of God's favor. If the rich could hardly get in, who could?

He said similar things often. "Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation" (Luke 6:24). "You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24), and the word is cannot. He told of a farmer whose land produced so well that he tore down his barns to build bigger ones, and God called him a fool the night he died. Notice what the man is not accused of. He didn't cheat anyone. His land did well. His whole offense is in the pronouns: my crops, my barns, my grain, my goods, my soul. He told of another rich man, dressed in purple, who feasted every day while a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate. That man isn't accused of doing anything to Lazarus either. He stepped over him for years, and that was enough.

But the same Gospels show Jesus doing other things, and a full reading has to include them. He did not tell everyone to sell everything. Zacchaeus, a wealthy tax collector, announced that he was giving half his goods to the poor and repaying fourfold anyone he had cheated, and Jesus said, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9). He gave half and kept the rest. Jesus' own work was paid for by women of means, "who provided for them out of their means" (Luke 8:3). The man who buried him was "a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus" (Matthew 27:57). And when the disciples asked who could be saved, his answer was not that the rich are shut out. It was, "With man it is impossible, but not with God" (Mark 10:27).

## The First Churches

The book of Acts describes a church in Jerusalem where "no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common" (Acts 4:32). People sold land and houses and brought the money to the apostles, and the result was that "there was not a needy person among them" (4:34). That sentence echoes a promise in the law of Moses about what Israel would look like if it obeyed. Luke is saying the promise had begun to come true.

It was not a rule. When a man named Ananias sold a field and lied about how much he was giving, Peter told him, "While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?" (Acts 5:4). He was free to keep it. What the first Christians did, they did because they wanted to, and that makes it harder to dismiss.

Paul's churches included people with large houses, and he never told them to give the houses up. What he told Timothy was this: "As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share" (1 Timothy 6:17–18). There were rich Christians, and they were given orders. In the same chapter he warned that "those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare" (6:9), and that "the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils" (6:10). Paul says a root, and he says the love of money. The warning is aimed at wanting it, which the poor can do as well as the rich.

James, the brother of the Lord, is the least patient. "Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you" (James 5:1). His charge is specific. They have held back the pay of the workers who harvested their fields, and "the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts" (5:4).

## Two Old Answers

By about the year 200 the church had wealthy members in its great cities, and some of them were frightened by Mark 10. In Alexandria a teacher named Clement wrote a short work for them called *Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?* His answer became one of the two great Christian positions. Jesus, he argued, was after the man's attachment and not his bank balance. A person can give away everything and still be eaten up with wanting it. Wealth is a tool. "Riches, then, which benefit also our neighbours, are not to be thrown away," he wrote, and "Such an instrument is wealth." A tool can be used well or badly, and the person holding it is the one who answers for it.

That is the stewardship tradition, and at its best it is demanding. It says that nothing you have is finally yours. You hold it in trust, and you will be asked what you did with it. John Wesley, in the eighteenth century, gave it the form most Protestants know. He told his Methodists to gain all they could by honest work and to save all they could by plain living, and then came the part that made the first two safe: "Having first gained all you can, and secondly saved all you can, then give all you can."

The other answer is older in spirit and never went away. Around 270 a young Egyptian named Antony, rich by the standards of his village, heard the story of the rich man read in church and took the words as spoken to him. He gave away what he had and went into the desert, and the monastic movement followed him. This tradition says that Clement makes it too easy. Of course attachment is the problem, but who among us is the exception whose heart stays free while his barns fill? Jesus said "sell," and a man walked away from him over it. The surest way to stop loving money is to stop having it.

The preachers of the fourth century stood between the two and gave neither any rest. John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch on the rich man and Lazarus, told his congregation to remember one thing above all: "that not to share our own riches with the poor is a robbery of the poor, and a depriving them of their livelihood; and that that which we possess is not only our own, but also theirs." He did not say the wealthy had stolen their money. He said that keeping it was the theft. In Cappadocia, Basil of Caesarea fed the starving during a famine and then built, outside his city, a complex of buildings to house the sick and the poor. His friend Gregory of Nazianzus described it after his death: "Go forth a little way from the city, and behold the new city, the storehouse of piety, the common treasury of the wealthy, in which the superfluities of their wealth, aye, and even their necessaries, are stored, in consequence of his exhortations." Basil had not told the rich of Caesarea that their money was evil. He had preached until they built a hospital with it.

## The Prosperity Teaching

In the last century a third answer appeared, and it has to be named plainly because it has spread across the world. It teaches that God wills financial prosperity for every believer, that faith is the means of getting it, and that giving, especially to the ministry doing the teaching, is the seed that produces the harvest. If you are still poor, or still sick, the fault lies in your faith.

It is worth understanding why people believe it before saying why it is false. It tells poor people that God cares about their rent and their children's shoes, which is true, and which many comfortable churches have forgotten how to say. It takes the Bible's promises of provision seriously. It expects God to act. Much of the scorn poured on it comes from people who have never needed a miracle to make it to Friday, and they should be slow to mock those who have.

But it is an error, and a grave one. It turns God into a means and money into the end, which is the exact reversal Jesus warned about. Paul described teachers who were "imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:5), and he was not complimenting them. It can't account for the apostles, who died poor, or for Paul, who said he had learned to be content "facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need" (Philippians 4:12). It can't account for Jesus, who "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9). And its cruelty falls on the people least able to bear it. The widow who gives her grocery money and stays poor is told that she is the problem. The preacher's house grows, and James's harvesters are still crying out. This is said with grief, because the people in those seats are our brothers and sisters, and what they came looking for was God.

## The Opposite Pride

The critic of the prosperity gospel has a temptation of his own, and it gets less attention because it looks like virtue.

There is a pride of the modest income. It keeps a careful watch on other people's cars and vacations. It knows exactly how much is too much, and the line always falls a little above what it has. It talks about justice and feels something closer to envy. When a woman poured expensive ointment on Jesus, one disciple objected that the money could have gone to the poor, and John tells us he said it "not because he cared about the poor" (John 12:6). Concern for the poor can be a costume too.

Scripture doesn't treat poverty as holiness. The writer of Proverbs prays, "give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you and say, 'Who is the LORD?' or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God" (Proverbs 30:8–9). Both conditions have their temptations. A person can renounce everything and be proud of it, and a person can own very little and think about money all day.

## What Is Fixed and What Is Open

Some things here are not open. God cannot be bought, and his favor cannot be measured in dollars. Any teaching that makes prosperity the promise of the gospel has changed the gospel. Greed is a sin on the same lists as adultery, though it is almost never treated that way. The care of the poor is a command.

Beyond that, Christians have real freedom and real disagreement. How much may a believer keep? Is giving it all away a calling for some or the plain meaning for all? The monastery and the merchant have both been in the church since the third century, and the church has canonized people from each. No creed settles it. That freedom is a place where each of us has to answer to God without a number to hide behind, and most of us would prefer the number.

The church's own hands are not clean. James had to tell the first congregations to stop giving the man with the gold ring the good seat and telling the poor man to stand (James 2:2–3), and we have been giving the good seat to the gold ring ever since. We have named buildings for donors and softened sermons for them. We have preached the tithe to people with nothing and said very little to people with a great deal. We have built ourselves handsome things with money given for the poor, in more than one century.

Mark never says what became of the man who ran up to Jesus and knelt. He went away sorrowful, and the story moves on. But Mark does say that Jesus looked at him and loved him, and said the hard thing because of it.

That look is on everyone who reads the passage and starts working out why it doesn't apply.

*"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."* (Matthew 6:21)

*"For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich."* (2 Corinthians 8:9)
